title: Call-by-push-value
text:
The CBPV paradigm is based on the slogan "a value is, a computation does". One complication in the presentation is distinguishing type variables ranging over value types from those ranging over computation types. This article follows Levy in using underlines to denote computations, so B is an (arbitrary) value type but \underline{B} is a computation type.[1] Some authors use other conventions, such as distinct sets of letters.[2]

The exact set of constructs varies by author and desired use for the calculus, but the following constructs are typical:[3,1]

Lambdas λx.M are computations of type A \to \underline{B} , where x : A and M : \underline{B} . A lambda application F V or V'F is a computation of type \underline{B} , where V : A and F : A \to \underline{B} . The let-binding construct let { x_1 = V_1; ... }. M binds values x_1 to values V_1, of matching types A_1 , inside a computation M : \underline{B} .

A thunk thunk M is a value of type U \underline{A} constructed from a computation M of type \underline{A} . Forcing a thunk is a computation, force X : \underline{A} for a thunk X : U \underline{A} .

It is also possible to wrap a value V of type A as a computation return V : F A . Such a computation can be used inside another computation as M to x. N : \underline{B} , where M : F A , and N : \underline{B} is a computation.

Values can also include algebraic data types constructed from a tag and zero or more sub-values, while computations include a deconstructing pattern-match match V as { (1,...) in M_1, ... }. Depending on presentation, ADTs may be limited to binary sums and products, Booleans only, or be omitted altogether.

A program is a closed computation of type F A , where A is a ground ADT type.[1]

### Complex values

Expressions such as not true : bool make sense denotationally. But, following the rules above, not can only be encoded using pattern-matching, which would make it a computation, and therefore the overall expression must also be a computation, giving not true : F bool. Similarly, there is no way to obtain 1 from (1,2) without constructing a computation. When modelling CBPV in the equational or category theory, such constructs are indispensable. Levy therefore defines an extended IR, "CBPV with complex values". This IR extends let-binding to bind values within a value expression, and also to pattern-match a value with each clause returning a value expression.[4] Besides modelling, such constructs also make writing programs in CBPV more natural.[3]

Complex values complicate the operational semantics, in particular requiring an arbitrary decision of when to evaluate the complex value. Such a decision has no semantic significance because evaluating complex values has no side effects. Also, it is possible to syntactically convert any computation or closed expression to one of the same type and denotation without complex values.[4] Therefore, many presentations omit complex values.[1]
